title: India-New Zealand FTA Takes Effect Oct. 20 With Zero-Duty Indian Exports
excerpt: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal and his New Zealand counterpart confirmed the October 20 start date after both countries completed ratification, opening duty-free access for every Indian export to New Zealand.
body:
• The India–New Zealand free trade agreement enters into force on October 20, 2026, with 100% of Indian exports gaining duty-free access to New Zealand from day one.
  • Indian tariffs of up to 10% on New Zealand goods disappear for exporters; engineering exports are expected to double to $280–300 million over five years, EEPC India says.
  • Dairy stays protected: India conceded nothing on dairy, while apples, kiwifruit and Manuka honey face tariff-rate quotas with minimum import prices.
  • New Zealand committed to facilitating $20 billion of investment into India over 15 years, and the pact covers services, professional mobility and student pathways.

New Delhi's trade establishment marked a milestone on September 21 as Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal and New Zealand Trade and Investment Minister Todd McClay confirmed that the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement will come into force on October 20, coinciding with Vijay Dashami. The announcement, made during a virtual conference, followed the completion of ratification in both countries and ends a six-month wait since the pact was signed at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on April 27, 2026.

Nine months of negotiation, six months of waiting

The agreement was negotiated in a brisk nine months, but needed New Zealand's Parliament to pass implementing legislation before it could operate. That hurdle was cleared on September 16, when lawmakers in Wellington approved the legislation by 93 votes to 29 with cross-party support. Both countries then formally completed ratification on September 21, allowing diplomatic notes to be exchanged and the entry-into-force date to be locked in.

For India, the deal is the latest in a run of bilateral pacts — following agreements with Australia and the United Arab Emirates — aimed at diversifying export markets as global supply chains realign. Bilateral goods trade stood at about $1.15 billion in FY26, with goods and services together near $2.29 billion, a modest base both sides want to multiply.

What exporters gain on day one

The headline commitment is unambiguous: every tariff line covering 100% of India's exports to New Zealand becomes duty-free the day the pact takes effect. That covers labour-intensive sectors where India has deep capacity — textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, engineering goods, processed foods, automobiles and auto components, and gems and jewellery. Before the agreement, some Indian products faced New Zealand tariffs of up to 10%, and Goyal noted their removal eliminates a disadvantage Indian exporters faced against competitors already entrenched in that market.

India also locked in services commitments across IT and IT-enabled services, professional services, education, financial services, tourism and construction, alongside provisions on investment and mobility for professionals, students and young people.

The engineering-export multiplier

The zero-duty access is expected to have its sharpest effect on engineering goods, one of the fastest-growing categories in India's export basket to New Zealand. Engineering shipments have already risen about 8% to $140.5 million in 2025–26, led by automobiles, dairy-sector machinery and medical and scientific instruments, plus iron, steel, aluminium and zinc products.

"With zero-duty access and predictable trade rules, there is a clear opportunity to scale up engineering exports to around $280–300 million over the next five years."

— Pankaj Chadha, Chairman, EEPC India

Chadha said the pact provides a strong tailwind particularly for micro, small and medium enterprises by lowering trade barriers and guaranteeing stable access in a relatively small but high-potential market. FIEO's Ajay Sahai added that the agreement gives fresh momentum to Indian exporters seeking diversification in the Indo-Pacific market.

What India kept off the table

The concessions are not symmetric, and the asymmetry is deliberate. India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on around 95% of New Zealand's exports by value — roughly 57% becoming tariff-free immediately — but kept its sensitive sectors closed. Dairy received no market access concessions, except for re-exports and bulk infant formula. Onions, chickpeas, peas, maize, almonds, artificial honey, sugar and edible oils also stay protected.

New Zealand's signature products — apples, kiwifruit and Manuka honey — were granted tariff-rate quotas with minimum import prices and seasonal import windows instead of outright liberalisation, plus safeguards for domestic farmers. Wine tariffs will decline over a longer phase-out period. Wool, meat, coal and forestry products get a cleaner path into India. To sweeten the agriculture chapter, the two sides created an Agriculture Productivity Partnership with dedicated action plans for kiwifruit, apples and honey, and centres of excellence for orchard management, post-harvest practices, supply chains, food safety and sustainable beekeeping.

The $20 billion bet

Beyond tariffs, New Zealand committed to facilitating $20 billion of investment into India over the next 15 years — a pledge New Zealand High Commissioner to India Patrick John Rata called a "huge" development for both countries, framing the pact as a decision by two countries to trust each other.

"Both New Zealand and India can be proud of the very high quality agreement that will deliver significant benefits for the citizens of our two countries."

— Todd McClay, New Zealand Minister for Trade and Investment

With the investment commitment, services chapter and mobility framework sitting alongside the tariff elimination, the deal reads as a comprehensive economic partnership rather than a simple tariff bargain. Whether the October 20 date marks the start of a genuine trade surge — particularly for the MSME engineering exporters EEPC is counting on — will show up first in the customs data of the quarter after entry into force.

The ministers announced on September 21 that the India–New Zealand free trade agreement will enter into force on October 20, 2026.
nri_angle: Indian exporters — including MSME owners in the diaspora who source or distribute through India — gain zero-duty access to New Zealand from October 20, with engineering goods the biggest beneficiary.
